result: TMS and tES are FDA-approved treatments with established clinical applications and have been used for both therapeutic purposes in clinical populations and cognitive enhancement in healthy individuals.
evaluation: Claims C1-C3 are well-supported by multiple citations to peer-reviewed literature (Hallett, 2007; Walsh and Cowey, 2000; Grover et al., 2021; Khedr et al., 2005; McGough et al., 2019; Santarnecchi et al., 2015). These claims establish the background context for the study and represent established knowledge in the field.

result: Despite promising results, contradictory findings have emerged across TMS and tES studies, and participants consistently report perceptual sensations during stimulation. Sham protocols have been developed to control for these non-specific effects by mimicking perceptual sensations without affecting cortical excitability.
evaluation: Claims C4-C8 are supported by appropriate citations documenting inconsistent findings (Horvath et al., 2015; Medina and Cason, 2017; Parkin et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2018; Westwood et al., 2017), perceptual sensations (Davis et al., 2013), and sham protocol development (Fonteneau et al., 2019; Gandiga et al., 2006; Fritsch et al., 2010; Nitsche and Paulus, 2000). These claims establish the rationale for examining subjective beliefs.

result: In Study 1 (treatment-resistant depression, N=121), subjective treatment (participants' beliefs about receiving active vs. sham rTMS) explained variability in depression scores over time better than objective treatment allocation, with participants believing they received active treatment showing steeper decreases in depression.
evaluation: Claims C9-C14 present a coherent analysis with appropriate statistical tests (linear mixed models), significant p-values (p<0.001), and model fit metrics (AIC, BIC). The two-way interaction between subjective treatment and time was significant, while objective treatment did not improve model fit when subjective treatment was included. The statistical approach is sound and results are clearly reported.

result: In Study 1, subjective treatment better predicted response rates on both HAMD-17 and BDI-II depression scales compared to objective treatment, with participants believing they received active treatment showing significantly higher response rates.
evaluation: Claims C15-C20 demonstrate consistent findings across two depression measures using appropriate binomial models. Statistical significance is reported with proper metrics (deviance, log odds ratios, p-values all <0.01). The replication across two scales strengthens the finding. Objective treatment did not improve model fit when subjective treatment was included (p>0.4 for both scales).

result: In Study 1, survival analysis of remission rates showed that subjective treatment significantly predicted remission (p<0.001), while objective treatment did not (p=0.053), with patients believing they received active stimulation showing higher remission rates.
evaluation: Claims C21-C24 use appropriate survival analysis methods (Gehan-Breslow-Wilcoxon test) for time-to-remission data. The contrast between non-significant objective treatment (p=0.053) and highly significant subjective treatment (p<0.001) is compelling. The operational definition of remission (HAMD-17 ≤7) is clearly stated.

result: In Study 2 (late-life depression, N=52, deep rTMS), a three-way interaction between subjective treatment, objective treatment, and time significantly predicted depression outcomes, with the steepest improvement occurring in patients who received active treatment but believed they received sham. Notably, subjective beliefs were assessed after week 1, before clinical changes emerged.
evaluation: Claims C25-C33 present a more complex pattern than Study 1, with a significant three-way interaction (p=0.011). The statistical analyses include appropriate contrasts and polynomial analyses. Critically, C27 and C64 note that subjective beliefs were assessed early (week 1), with significant effects emerging at weeks 3-4, supporting a causal interpretation. The counterintuitive finding (best outcomes in active/subjective-sham group) is well-documented statistically.

result: In Study 2, the interaction between subjective and objective treatment significantly predicted both remission and response rates, with higher rates observed when patients who received active treatment believed they received sham.
evaluation: Claims C34-C41 extend the Study 2 findings to binary outcomes using appropriate binomial models. The two-way interactions are significant for both remission (p=0.035) and response (p=0.004). The pattern replicates the continuous outcome findings, with the active-objective/sham-subjective group showing the best outcomes. Statistical parameters are properly reported.

result: In Study 3 (ADHD, N=64, home-based tDCS), both subjective treatment and objective treatment independently contributed to explaining variability in inattention symptoms, with subjective treatment showing significant effects (p<0.001) but not fully overruling objective treatment effects.
evaluation: Claims C42-C49 demonstrate a different pattern from Studies 1 and 2, where both subjective and objective treatment contributed significantly. The statistical analyses are appropriate (linear mixed models), and the finding that objective treatment remained significant even when subjective treatment was included (p<0.001) is clearly documented. This represents an important boundary condition for the main hypothesis.

result: In Study 4 (healthy adults, N=150, tDCS and mind-wandering), subjective treatment and subjective dosage both significantly predicted mind-wandering outcomes better than objective treatment, with mind-wandering increasing proportionally with perceived stimulation intensity.
evaluation: Claims C50-C58 extend findings to a non-clinical population and cognitive outcomes. Statistical analyses are appropriate, with subjective treatment (p=0.045) and subjective dosage (p=0.025) both significant, while objective treatment was not (p>0.09). The dose-response relationship for subjective dosage (C55-C56) provides additional evidence for the role of beliefs. This demonstrates generalizability beyond clinical populations.

result: Across all four studies, participants' subjective beliefs about treatment allocation explained variability in outcomes, with different patterns emerging: Studies 1 and 4 showed subjective treatment dominating objective treatment, Study 2 showed an interaction effect with best outcomes in the active-objective/sham-subjective group, and Study 3 showed both factors contributing independently.
evaluation: Claims C59-C62 accurately summarize the main findings across studies. The variability in patterns (C63) is acknowledged as speculative but reasonable. The summary is consistent with the detailed statistical results presented for each study. However, C63's speculation about explanatory factors (personality, disorder type, etc.) lacks empirical support in the current data.

result: In Study 2, the temporal sequence of assessment (subjective beliefs at week 1, clinical changes at weeks 3-4) supports a causal interpretation where beliefs affected outcomes rather than vice versa.
evaluation: Claim C64 makes an important methodological point about temporal precedence in Study 2. The claim is supported by the study design (C27, C81) where subjective beliefs were assessed after the first week, with significant effects emerging 2-3 weeks later. This temporal sequence strengthens causal inference, though the authors appropriately note this is not definitive proof of causation.

result: Placebo effects can impact both behavior and brain activity, and most RCTs rely on self-reported outcomes. Expectations about treatment effectiveness can significantly modulate treatment effects.
evaluation: Claims C65-C67 are supported by appropriate citations (Fonteneau et al., 2019; Hashmi, 2018; Oken et al., 2008; Schmidt et al., 2014; Parong et al., 2022) and represent established knowledge. These claims provide important context for interpreting the main findings and their clinical relevance.

result: Study 1 methodology: 121 patients with treatment-resistant depression received rTMS (bilateral, unilateral, or sham) 5 times/week for 3-6 weeks using a Magventure system with appropriate sham controls, with subjective treatment assessed at study end.
evaluation: Claims C68-C73 provide methodological details for Study 1 that are clearly described and consistent with standard rTMS protocols. The adaptive design (remitters stop at week 3, non-remitters continue to week 6) is clearly explained. The sham protocol (coil angled 90°) is appropriate for blinding. These are factual descriptions of the study design.

result: Study 2 methodology: 52 older adults with late-life depression received deep rTMS (H1 coil) or sham 5 days/week for 4 weeks using a Brainsway system with appropriate sham controls, with subjective treatment assessed after the first week.
evaluation: Claims C74-C81 provide methodological details for Study 2. The deep rTMS protocol is well-described with specific parameters (18 Hz, 120% RMT, 6012 pulses/session). The sham control using a separate coil positioned above the scalp is appropriate. The key methodological difference from Study 1 (early assessment of subjective beliefs at week 1) is clearly stated and important for interpretation.

result: Study 3 methodology: 64 adults with ADHD received home-based tDCS (2 mA, 30 min/day) or sham for 4 weeks (28 sessions) targeting bilateral DLPFC with appropriate sham controls and impedance monitoring, with subjective treatment assessed at study end.
evaluation: Claims C82-C86 provide methodological details for Study 3. The home-based tDCS device with impedance monitoring and session tracking represents appropriate quality control for unsupervised administration. The electrode placement (F3/F4) and stimulation parameters (2 mA, 30 min) are standard. The sham protocol (brief ramp-up/down at beginning, middle, and end) is more elaborate than typical tDCS shams.

result: Study 4 methodology: 150 healthy adults received single-session tDCS at different intensities (1, 1.5, 2 mA) or sham targeting left prefrontal cortex, followed by a sustained attention task measuring mind-wandering, with both subjective treatment and subjective dosage assessed at study end. The study was single-blinded.
evaluation: Claims C87-C97 provide methodological details for Study 4. The single-session design differs from the multi-week protocols in Studies 1-3. The SART task with TUT probes is a validated measure of mind-wandering. The assessment of both subjective treatment and subjective dosage is a strength. However, C92 notes single-blinding (experimenters aware of condition), which could introduce bias through experimenter effects.

result: Statistical analyses used linear mixed-effects models (lme4 package) for continuous outcomes, which allow pooling of baseline means and accommodate correlated errors with unequal variances.
evaluation: Claims C98-C100 describe the statistical approach with appropriate citations (Bates et al., 2015; Laird and Ware, 1982). The advantages of mixed models over standard linear models are correctly stated. This represents appropriate methodology for the repeated-measures data structure in Studies 1-3.

result: Data and analysis code are publicly available on the Open Science Framework.
evaluation: Claim C101 states data availability, which is verifiable and represents good open science practice. This supports reproducibility of the analyses.
